episodes.title: Deborah Green Denied a Dying Boy Food and a Doctor
episodes.description:
Deborah Green spent four decades as the self-declared "General" of a paramilitary religious group that began in Sacramento as Free Love Ministries and became the Aggressive Christianity Missions Training Corps. In 2014, a 12-year-old boy named Enoch Miller died on her compound in Fence Lake, New Mexico, after she punished his illness by withholding food and controlling who was allowed to get him medical help. She has never been convicted of anything naming his death.

James and Deborah Green founded the group together in the early 1980s, after both had worked for the Salvation Army, and modeled it on that structure: uniforms, ranks, and a chain of command. By the mid-1980s, Deborah had declared that God spoke directly through her, and used that claim to hold the group's money, settle disputes, assign punishments, and decide who was allowed to leave or see a doctor. The group relocated repeatedly over the following decade before settling on an isolated compound in western New Mexico. In August 2017, Cibola County sheriff's deputies raided that compound on a Sunday morning and arrested Deborah in the middle of her own sermon, nineteen months after two members of the group had reported a death on the compound to police. A 2018 jury convicted her of kidnapping, criminal sexual penetration of a minor, and child abuse, and sentenced her to 72 years. That sentence was later thrown out after prosecutors were found to have withheld evidence from the defense, and the charges were ultimately dismissed. In a separate case built specifically around Enoch Miller's death, Deborah pleaded no contest to abuse of a child resulting in great bodily harm and was sentenced to 18 years; she served under four years. That conviction was vacated too, in 2022. In April 2025, the New Mexico Supreme Court unanimously reversed her release. By the time a bench warrant was issued that August, Deborah Green had already disappeared. 

Acts of the Faithful documents crimes and cover-ups committed by religious leaders and unstitutions, using court records, public filings, and on-record testimony.

episodes.title: River Road Fellowship's Prophet Was a Fugitive
episodes.description:
Victor Barnard spent over a decade running River Road Fellowship, an isolated religious community in rural Minnesota, before he was charged with sexually abusing children under his authority as the group's self-declared spiritual leader.

In 2000, Barnard told his congregation at Shepherd's Camp that God required their firstborn daughters. Ten girls, some as young as twelve, were separated from their families and placed into a group he called Alamoth. According to the criminal complaint later filed against him, Barnard told the girls he represented Christ in the flesh and that having sex with him was simply following God's word. Lindsay Tornambe told police the abuse began when she was thirteen and continued for nine years. A second victim, Jess Schlinsky, said hers began at twelve and lasted eight. The fellowship fractured in 2008 after members learned Barnard was also sleeping with several of the congregation's married women, and by 2009 what remained of the group, maidens included, had relocated to a house outside Spokane, Washington. When Tornambe first reported the abuse to Pine County authorities in 2012, the prosecutor at the time dismissed it as one person's word against another's, and no charges followed. It took a 2014 television investigation by Fox 9 in Minneapolis, with both women willing to go on camera, before prosecutors filed fifty nine counts of criminal sexual conduct against Barnard. He fled Spokane before he could be arrested and was found by Brazilian police in February 2015, living in a beachfront apartment in the resort town of Pipa. It took sixteen more months of extradition proceedings before he was returned to Pine County, Minnesota.

This video traces River Road Fellowship from its founding through Barnard's 2016 guilty plea and thirty year sentence, and the 2017 lawsuit Tornambe filed against fifteen of the fellowship's former elders for standing by while it happened.

Acts of the Faithful investigates documented cases of abuse and institutional failure inside religious organizations, working from primary court records and contemporaneous reporting rather than secondhand accounts.

episodes.title: The Cult Where Craig Mack Died
episodes.description:
Ralph Gordon Stair founded the Overcomer Ministry in 1978, a religious compound outside Walterboro, South Carolina, that broadcast his sermons on more than a hundred shortwave and digital radio stations while investigators looked into the deaths of infants born on the property and two separate criminal sexual conduct cases were brought against him.

Stair called himself the last prophet God would send to Earth, and used that claim to demand total control over the people who lived on his compound. Members cut ties with family outside the property, women wore only ministry-approved dresses, and children were raised on a curriculum that skipped science and left them without a diploma. Stair preached that seeing a doctor was a sin, and that doctrine extended to childbirth: through the 1980s and into the 1990s, several infants died during home births or shortly after, and sheriff's records confirm investigations took place, though no conviction ever followed. In 2002, two women told the Colleton County Sheriff's Office that Stair had raped them; he pleaded down to two misdemeanor counts in 2004 and served 77 days before returning to broadcasts that never stopped airing. In 2017, he was charged again, this time with eight felonies including three counts of first degree criminal sexual conduct.

One of the people living on the compound during these years was Craig Mack, best known for the 1994 single "Flava in Ya Ear," one of Bad Boy Records' first releases. Mack left the music industry in 2011 and joined Stair's compound, a move his family and fans learned about from a leaked video the following year. He told people in 2014 that he had congestive heart failure. He died on the compound in March 2018 at age 47, and his family said his heart had given out. It hadn't. A 2024 Rolling Stone investigation and Mack's own death certificate showed the real cause was untreated HIV and AIDS, a diagnosis his family says he likely knew about even before he arrived at the compound, one the ministry's total rejection of modern medicine ensured he would never be pushed to treat.

Stair died in 2021 while still under house arrest awaiting trial on the 2017 felony charges, and his death closed the case without a verdict. His estate kept the broadcasts running for a few more years before letting the syndication contracts lapse in 2025. The compound is still occupied, and by the ministry's own account, recordings of Stair's sermons still play there today.

Acts of the Faithful covers documented cases where religious authority was used to justify abuse, cover up wrongdoing, or avoid accountability, drawn from court records, sheriff's reports, and other primary documentation.

episodes.title: Nachman Helbrans Kidnapped His Own Niece for Lev Tahor
episodes.description:
Shlomo Helbrans founded Lev Tahor, a breakaway Hasidic sect that isolated its followers from mainstream Judaism and demanded total separation from the outside world. When Helbrans drowned in Mexico in July 2017, his son Nachman Helbrans took control, and under his leadership the group's abuses escalated from insular extremism into organized crime.

The group's record of documented harm predates Nachman's rule. In 2012, Quebec's child welfare authorities investigated the compound and found untreated skin infections and rotted teeth among the children, and a judge ordered fourteen children removed. By 2017, an Israeli court had already declared Lev Tahor a dangerous cult, citing physical abuse and the marriage of minors to spouses decades older.

Nachman ran the group through fear, physical brutality, and a management council called the Hanhala, while forcing members into unpaid labor and stripping them of savings and identity documents. Girls in the group were married off as young as thirteen. When his sister Sara Feige Teller fled the sect's Guatemala compound in 2018 and won custody of her children in a Brooklyn family court, Nachman responded by ordering a transnational kidnapping. Operatives abducted two of Sara's children, fourteen-year-old Yante and twelve-year-old Chaim, from a home in New York and smuggled them to Mexico to return Yante to the husband she had been forced to marry as a child.

The kidnapping triggered a three-week, multi-agency manhunt. Interpol and the FBI arrested Nachman and his lieutenant Mayer Rosner in Mexico, and in March 2022 a federal court sentenced both men to twelve years for kidnapping and child exploitation. The conviction did not end Lev Tahor. In December 2024, Guatemalan authorities raided the group's compound and documented child rape and forced pregnancies among underage girls, only for the group to storm the government shelter days later and reclaim most of the children through the country's own civil courts.

This video traces how a self-declared rabbi's isolated religious movement became, under his son's leadership, a documented criminal network that continues operating across Central America today.

Acts of the Faithful covers documented wrongdoing inside religious and institutional organizations, using court records, government investigations, and survivor testimony as its primary sources.

episodes.title: Gloriavale's Doctrine That Silenced Victims.
episodes.description:
Description:
In New Zealand's remote Haupiri Valley sits Gloriavale, the closed Christian settlement whose look partly inspired the costumes of Hulu's The Handmaid's Tale. Costume designer Ane Crabtree has said Gloriavale was one of the real-world religious groups she researched, alongside Amish dress and Shintoism, while building the visual world of Gilead. Behind that recognizable look, this documentary traces how one man's absolute authority as "Overseeing Shepherd" built a system designed to keep abuse, forced labor, and total isolation hidden from state oversight for over fifty years, in a settlement most of New Zealand has never been allowed to see inside.

Founded in 1969 by Australian evangelist Neville Cooper, later known to his followers as Hopeful Christian, the community relocated to its current 2,300 acre site on New Zealand's West Coast in the early 1990s. Cooper was convicted in 1994 of ten counts of indecent assault against children aged 12 to 17. He served eleven months in prison before returning to lead the community for another twenty four years, until his death in 2018.

His successor, Howard Temple, ran Gloriavale until his forced resignation in August 2025. That same year, Temple pleaded guilty to twelve charges of sexual and common assault against women and girls aged nine to twenty. A court sentenced him to prison time, but the High Court later overturned that sentence entirely, citing his age and a diagnosis of cognitive impairment, and replaced it with eleven months of home detention.

This video documents how Gloriavale's internal system handled abuse reports for decades, how New Zealand Police investigations, Operation Minneapolis and Operation Mathius, eventually identified dozens of alleged offenders and more than one hundred potential victims, and how the community's labor practices and banking relationships are now unraveling through New Zealand's Employment Court and Court of Appeal. It draws on court rulings, the Royal Commission of Inquiry's findings, and Gloriavale's own submissions to lay out what happened when one institution answered to no one but itself for over fifty years.

Acts of the Faithful covers documented institutional failure: organizations, and the individuals who ran them, that were given unchecked authority and the consequences that followed when that authority went unexamined for too long.

episodes.title: The American Cult Where Children Were Raised in Captivity
episodes.description:
Dwight York ran the Nuwaubian Nation of Moors — an American religious cult — for 35 years. In 2002, a federal raid on his compound in Eatonton, Georgia uncovered evidence of systematic child abuse spanning decades. York was convicted on 11 of 13 federal counts including racketeering conspiracy and Mann Act violations for transporting minors across state lines for sexual abuse. He was sentenced to 135 years. He is currently held at ADX Florence, the federal supermax in Florence, Colorado.
This video covers the full arc of York's organization: from the Ansaar Pure Sufi in 1967 Brooklyn, through the Nubian Islamic Hebrew Mission, to the Holy Tabernacle Ministries, to the Nuwaubian Nation of Moors and the 476-acre Tama-Re compound in rural Georgia. It examines how York rebuilt the organization's entire belief system four times while maintaining absolute authority over the same followers — and what that loyalty reveals about how high-control religious organizations actually function.
Topics covered: the organizational history of the Nuwaubian Nation of Moors, the construction of the Tama-Re compound, the FBI investigation and its repeated suppression, the 2002 federal raid, the trial and conviction of Dwight York, and the analytical case that the theology was always a cover for the authority structure beneath it.
Acts of the Faithful is a channel built on accountability journalism applied to religious institutions, movements, and figures.

episodes.title: The Church With a Cemetery Full of Children.
episodes.description:
In a Clackamas County cemetery in Oregon City, dozens of children are buried in graves marked with no names. Just designations. The Followers of Christ church has practiced faith healing for over a century — refusing medicine, substituting prayer and olive oil, and watching children die of conditions that would have resolved with basic medical care.
Between 2009 and 2025, Clackamas County prosecutors secured six criminal convictions against Followers of Christ parents for faith healing deaths and medical neglect. The cases include the deaths of 15-month-old Ava Worthington, 16-year-old Neil Beagley, newborns David Hickman and Ginnifer Mitchell, and infant Hayden Edwards. The victims died of pneumonia, urinary tract blockage, respiratory distress, and other treatable conditions while family members prayed and anointed them with olive oil.
In 2011 Oregon passed House Bill 2721, eliminating the religious exemption that had shielded faith healing parents from homicide charges. The church's response was not reform. Several hundred members relocated to Canyon County, Idaho, where state statute explicitly protects parents who choose prayer over medical treatment for their children. No successful prosecution of a Followers of Christ member for faith healing neglect has occurred in Idaho.
A 2023 study found that 33 percent of graves in the Followers of Christ's Peaceful Valley Cemetery in Canyon County belong to children. The statewide average is 3 percent.
This is an accountability journalism channel covering religious fraud, institutional cover-ups, and documented crimes committed under the cover of faith.

episodes.title: How Gateway Church Protected a Child Predator for 43 Years
episodes.description:
In 1982, Robert Morris sexually abused a 12-year-old girl. He went on to found Gateway Church, one of the largest megachurches in America, serve as a spiritual adviser to Donald Trump, and preach to 26,000 people a week.

In 2025, he pleaded guilty to five counts of lewd or indecent acts with a child. He served six months.

This video is not about what Robert Morris did. It is about the doctrine that made all of it possible. Biblical restoration is a formal framework in evangelical church governance that allows a leader who has committed a sin to be privately adjudicated, supervised, and cleared for return to ministry — without criminal process, without external accountability, and without the victim's knowledge or consent.

Gateway Church's elders received a letter in 2007 that named Cindy Clemishire's age and the date the abuse began. They convened a special meeting. They concluded the restoration was sufficient. They did not contact law enforcement. Morris's standing was unchanged.

That was not a failure of culture. That was a decision.

Cindy Clemishire waited 43 years.

Acts of the Faithful covers religious fraud, institutional cover-ups, and the gap between what faith organizations claim to stand for and what the record shows they actually did.

episodes.title: America Watched Him Get Caught. He Got Richer
episodes.description:
In 1986, James Randi brought a radio scanner to a Peter Popoff revival and picked up a signal on 39.17 megahertz. It was Popoff's wife Elizabeth, reading names and medical conditions from prayer cards the audience had filled out before the service. Johnny Carson played the recording on national television. The ministry collapsed within a year. Popoff filed for bankruptcy in 1987 with nearly 800 creditors.

By 2005 he was pulling in $23 million a year. His infomercials were still running in 2025.

This video examines how a documented faith healing fraud survived a national exposure, rebuilt a larger operation, and converted it to a tax-exempt religious organization. The question isn't whether Peter Popoff is a fraud. That was settled in 1986 in front of millions of people. The question is what it means that it didn't matter.

Acts of the Faithful covers what religious institutions do when they think no one is watching. New video every week.

episodes.title: The Largest Church Ponzi Scheme in History
episodes.description:
Gerald Payne ran the largest church Ponzi scheme in American history. His Tampa ministry, Greater Ministries International, collected more than $400 million from 15,000 victims between 1996 and 1999.
The pitch: give $250 to the ministry and God would give you back $500. The program was backed by diamond mines in Liberia and the Greater International Bank of Nauru.
None of those things existed.
Victims included elderly Baptist congregations, Amish communities, and Mennonite families who mortgaged homes and liquidated retirement accounts to maximize their gifts. When returns never arrived, Payne told participants that questioning the program was the same as lacking faith in God. Many victims never called law enforcement. Every tool for self-protection had been reframed as a sin.
When Florida regulators moved to shut the program down, Payne's attorneys redesigned the documentation and took the case to court. Securities law requires a human being on the other end of a financial promise. Payne's attorneys put God there instead. In 1997, a Florida appellate court agreed.
Federal prosecutors came at it differently. They didn't argue about whether God could make a promise. They proved that everything behind the promise was invented.
In 2001, a federal jury convicted five Greater Ministries leaders following a six-week trial. U.S. District Judge James Whittemore sentenced Payne to 27 years and called the use of God's name to perpetuate the fraud absolutely despicable. The $400 million was never recovered.

Acts of the Faithful covers fraud, institutional failure, and documented wrongdoing in religious organizations.

episodes.title: The Government That Helped Build Her Empire
episodes.description:
Grace Road Church founder Shin Ok-ju built a business empire in Fiji using unpaid labor from her own congregation, and the Fijian government helped her do it. In October 2017, Prime Minister Frank Bainimarama personally presented the Grace Road Group with the country's Primary Industry Business Excellence Award. By then the church-owned conglomerate had already received millions of dollars in loans from Fiji's own development bank, a state institution created to support local Fijian small businesses.
Shin founded Grace Road in South Korea in 2002 on the claim that she alone could correctly interpret the Bible. Inside the church, she ran what she called the threshing floor: violent group sessions she framed as spiritual correction. When she began preaching that Fiji was the one place on earth that would survive an approaching apocalypse, roughly four hundred members sold their homes and businesses and relocated. On arrival, their passports were confiscated and their labor became the foundation of a conglomerate that eventually spanned more than fifty companies, from restaurants to dental clinics, while the members who built it worked without wages or freedom of movement.
The threshing floor didn't stop in Fiji. It surfaced publicly in 2018, when a South Korean television program aired leaked footage of Shin directing the beatings herself. She was arrested that same month and later convicted on charges including violence, fraud, and child abuse. Her son, Daniel Kim, took over the church's Fijian operations and is now in immigration detention, fighting deportation through the Fijian courts. Grace Road is still open. And Fiji is still exposed to a Tier 3 designation in the U.S. Trafficking in Persons report, a downgrade that would put roughly sixteen million dollars in annual aid at risk, along with the country's standing with lenders and trade partners well beyond that figure.
This video traces how a small Korean church became one of the most economically entangled religious organizations in the South Pacific, and what it cost a government to look the other way.

Acts of the Faithful investigates documented fraud, abuse, and institutional cover-ups across religious organizations, treating each case as a matter of public record rather than theological debate.

episodes.title: The Hare Krishna Guru Who Ordered a Murder to Hide Child Abuse
episodes.description:
On May 22, 1986, Steven Bryant was shot twice in the head while sitting in his van in Los Angeles. He had been publishing detailed accounts of financial corruption, sexual misconduct, and child molestation inside a Hare Krishna community. The man who ordered his killing was the community's spiritual leader.
This is the story of New Vrindaban, Kirtanananda Swami, and a school system that was designed from the start to operate beyond the reach of child welfare law.
ISKCON's gurukula boarding schools enrolled children as young as five, separated them from their parents, and placed them under the absolute authority of teachers the organization framed as spiritual fathers. In a 1976 letter, founder Prabhupada identified the risk of government scrutiny and proposed building schools in India as an escape from Western oversight. The American schools kept running. The abuse was systematic and documented across at least eight of ISKCON's eleven North American schools.
When Bryant began publishing what he had seen, Kirtanananda authorized a payment of $2,500 to have him located and killed. When the job was done, he authorized $6,000 more to help the killer flee the country.
In 1996, with his own enforcer testifying against him, Kirtanananda pleaded guilty to racketeering and conspiracy to murder. He was sentenced to twenty years.
His authority was absolute. His corruption was too.
